definition: Inhibitor means a substance or influence that slows or blocks a process — in science writing, the agent that binds part of the machinery so a reaction cannot run.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word inhibitor. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know inhibitor should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The pipeline owes its forty-year life to a corrosion inhibitor, a film of molecules that coats the steel and starves the rust of any purchase.
A damper is milder than an inhibitor: it takes the edge off a process that keeps on running, while an inhibitor grips the machinery and holds the process itself back.
A neutralizer goes further than an inhibitor: an inhibitor holds a process back and lets it resume when removed, while a neutralizer cancels the active agent outright, leaving nothing to restart.

A suppressant quiets an activity that is already raging — the cough, the appetite, the fever — without touching what drives it. An inhibitor reaches into the works: it binds a piece of the machinery so the process itself cannot run.

Inhibitor means a substance or influence that slows or blocks a process — in science writing, the agent that binds part of the machinery so a reaction cannot run.
The lab's best blood-pressure drug does nothing to the heart at all.

It is an inhibitor: its molecules fit into an enzyme's working slot the way a bent key fits a lock — snugly, and uselessly — so the enzyme can no longer produce the hormone that tightens blood vessels.
The vessels relax because a single step upstream has been quietly jammed.
Inhibitor is the precise word because the drug neither destroys the enzyme nor mops up the hormone after it forms; it holds one step of the process back, and everything downstream slows with it.
That is what inhibitors do in any laboratory sentence: they act on the machinery, not the aftermath.

Cut an apple and the browning begins within minutes: an enzyme meets the air and sets a chain of reactions running.
The packing plant's answer is an inhibitor, a food-safe compound dissolved in the rinse water.
It does not toughen the fruit or seal the slice; it binds one site on the enzyme itself, and with that grip in place the browning chain cannot start.
Rinse the compound away and the enzyme wakes; the slices brown by lunchtime.
The chemists like to say the fruit is never fought, only paused — the machinery is held, not broken.
